values: Best use: a real document or quote as proof (a page, a letter, a paper), with the quoted words highlighted. Limit: max 30% of runtime. Not for: a page with nothing highlighted or said about it.
Best use: one statistic or contrast that the line says out loud (two or three bars, one hero). Limit: max 6 beats per episode. Not for: numbers the narration doesn't say.
Best use: showing scale (many headlines or pages saying the same thing). Limit: max 3 beats per episode, at most one per act. Not for: a single source.
Best use: the first appearance of a named person or a hero subject. Limit: max 8 beats per episode. Not for: repeating a portrait already shown.
Best use: one small detail inside a crowded picture or page. Limit: max 8 beats per episode. Not for: a picture whose whole frame is the point.
Best use: web pages, specifications or museum records shown as evidence. Limit: max 6 beats per episode. Not for: text the narrator reads in full.
Best use: the turn into each act (chapter number and title). Limit: max 8 beats per episode. Not for: mid-act headings.

Two to four real pictures side by side as equal panels (image or muted clip), each with its label; on its word each panel takes a stamp (SAME) that locks on (MOT-003); the panels can dim back so names come forward, joined by a MOT-005 thread; one serif line above. Preview SplitComparisonCard-<theme>.

Best use: showing what stays the same against what changes (the flower, the candle and the stockings are the same; only the person looking changes). Limit: max 8 beats per episode; 2-4 panels, every panel a registered source. Not for: data with numbers (MinimalDataChart) or two versions of one picture (SwatchRows).

Best use: the one slow move on a still picture or a held shot (calm limit 3%). Limit: one move per shot; never stacked with another camera move. Not for: diagrams that already move.
Best use: entrances of headlines, labels, charts and underlines. Limit: one entrance per element; no beat cap (it is a motion rule, not a picture).
Best use: brackets, highlights and cards that lock on. Limit: one lock per element; no beat cap.
Best use: only inside HeadlineMatchCut (VIS-003). Limit: follows VIS-003 (max 3 beats per episode).

A line that draws itself from one thing to another (a route between two places, a thread between two names): a gentle bow, a head dot leading it, a ring settling on the end; dashed for routes; optional MOT-009 boil. Calm: 0.8-1.6 s, slow-out, one trace at a time. Preview VectorTraceConnector-<theme>.

Best use: a route between two places on a map (Eaglesfield to Kendal) or a link between two named things the line says belong together (John and Jonathan). Limit: max 6 beats per episode; one trace on screen at a time. Not for: decoration, or arrows that point at what a label already names.
Best use: the default cut between beats, keeping the focal point within 25% of the screen. Limit: no beat cap (it is the plain cut); use PushThrough or a slate only where they add meaning.

A ruled ink line is drawn straight across the frame by a pen nib, leaning about 8 degrees, like a draughtsman's rule; the new shot is already in place behind the line and is uncovered as it passes; the hairline stays 0.25 s, then fades. The J-cut half is in the act file: the next shot's own sound (page, room tone) starts 0.4-0.8 s before the wipe. Sound: SFX-017 InkLineFoley under the stroke. Episode transitionIn 'draft' {angle, dir}.

Best use: from a drawing or diagram into a document, or between two drawings, when the next shot's sound can lead in (a J-cut). Limit: max 4 per episode, never two in a row; 0.7-0.9 s. Not for: real photos of people, or calm reflective moments.
Own (23 Nov 2026; Sam: 'Build the transitions which we haven't built yet')

The whole old shot (a full-frame photo or page) shrinks and flies into the slot where it sits in the next layout (a card, a thumbnail, a place on a board or map), with a thin paper border and a soft shadow, while the next shot fades up round it; the new shot's own card takes over in the last 0.25 s. Episode transitionIn 'photocard' {rect: [x, y, w, h] in the new shot}.

Best use: a picture we were inside becoming one piece of a bigger picture (a page onto a board, a photo onto a map, a source into an evidence chain). Limit: max 3 per episode; the new shot must hold a real slot at rect; 0.8-1.0 s. Not for: a new shot with no matching slot.
Own (22 Nov 2026, both Vox-style Remotion demos; analysis only; built 23 Nov 2026)

Whip-pan between cards with directional blur then zoom-out to full contact grid. Also (22 Nov 2026, both Vox-style demos; analysis only): a locked stage, where the grid paper never moves inside a scene group and scenes change by their layers sliding out together, so a run reads as one continuous shot. Built 23 Nov 2026 as CanvasGridPan: the camera pulls back to 0.82, the gridded drafting sheet shows round both cards, it glides to the next card (blur at most 6 px at top speed) and pushes back in; 1.3 s. Episode transitionIn 'canvas' {dir, pull}. Sound: SFX-021 AirClothWhoosh on the glide.

Best use: runs of scenes on one idea inside an act. Limit: scene changes between ideas keep their designed transitions (TRN-006/007/011-013); max 4 per act, never two in a row; pull no deeper than 0.8.
Own (23 Nov 2026; Sam: 'Build the transitions which we haven't built yet')

A drop of ink lands at a point and spreads like ink in wet paper, with a ragged, fibrous edge (SVG turbulence on the mask, calming as it grows); the new shot shows through the ink. Optional tint: the ink carries a colour that means something for its first frames, then clears. 1.0 s, eased out. Episode transitionIn 'ink' {at, tint}. Sound: SFX-016 PaperFoley (soft) at -26 dB.

Best use: a change that spreads from one point, where the spreading means something (Dalton's blue tint, a stain, a dye, a rumour, a colour taking over). Limit: max 2 per episode, never two in a row; one drop only. Not for: a plain scene change with no spreading idea.
Best use: archive-led episodes (old papers, photos, maps). Limit: the episode's theme, chosen at Gate 0; one theme per episode.
